strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: scaling online reinforcement learning for multi-turn mobile GUI agents, where sparse rewards and expensive environment sampling are real bottlenecks.
The proposed MobileRL pipeline is practically meaningful, combining SFT warm-up, reasoning SFT, and online agentic RL in a way that addresses cold-start exploration and sample efficiency.

Empirical results are strong on the reported benchmarks, especially the claimed 80.2% success rate on AndroidWorld and 53.6% on AndroidLab, substantially exceeding listed open and proprietary baselines.
The paper includes useful component ablations for AdaPR, SPA, and FCF, plus stage-wise ablations showing the contribution of reasoning-free SFT, reasoning SFT, and RL.
The appendix provides nontrivial implementation details, including action space design, XML preprocessing, training hyperparameters, data sources, privacy filtering, and resource requirements.
weaknesses: The novelty of ADAGRPO is somewhat incremental: positive replay, curriculum filtering, and length-based reward shaping are sensible engineering choices, but the paper does not clearly establish a deep algorithmic contribution beyond adapting known ideas to mobile GUI RL.

There are concerning evaluation validity issues around AndroidLab. The appendix states that reward-model training uses traces from both training and test tasks, with test-task labels derived from the rule-based evaluator. Even if the final benchmark evaluation is rule-based, using test-task traces to train a reward model can leak test-distribution information into training and weakens the AndroidLab claims.

The training/evaluation split construction is not fully reassuring. AndroidWorld and AndroidLab training tasks are generated or expanded from the same benchmark environments/templates as evaluation tasks, and the paper mainly removes exact content/state overlap rather than demonstrating robust template-level or app-level generalization.

Baseline comparability is under-specified. It is unclear whether all baselines are rerun under the same environment versions, action space, image resolution, XML access, prompts, stopping criteria, and number of attempts, or whether many numbers are copied from prior reports.

The strongest reported models appear to use different training mixtures selected per backbone, and the paper reports the best setting for each. This complicates attribution and may overstate the generality of the method.

Statistical support is limited. Some ablations are averaged over three runs, but the main benchmark comparisons do not provide confidence intervals or significance tests despite small test sets of 116 and 138 tasks.

Reproducibility remains limited despite implementation details: the abstract has an empty open-source link, the distributed Android training setup requires very large compute, and some data/reward-model construction depends on proprietary VLMs and human verification.

The method relies heavily on XML accessibility metadata and benchmark-style emulator environments, and the authors explicitly do not evaluate on out-of-domain public-use apps. This limits the strength of claims about general mobile GUI agents.
The reward model for AndroidLab has only 86% accuracy and is trained from proprietary VLM majority votes, introducing possible bias and reward hacking risks that are not deeply analyzed.

Some presentation choices obscure key details, such as the exact AdaPR sampling behavior when gamma is 1.0, the permanent-removal criterion in FCF, and how filtering hard tasks affects the effective training objective.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: online reinforcement learning for multi-turn mobile GUI agents, where interactive sampling is expensive and sparse rewards are a real bottleneck.
The paper reports large empirical gains on AndroidWorld and AndroidLab, including stage-wise results for two backbones and some ablations for the proposed ADAGRPO components.

The system engineering effort for distributed Android environment sampling is potentially valuable, and the appendices include useful details on action space, XML preprocessing, training data composition, and resource constraints.
The authors acknowledge several limitations, including reward-model bias, lack of open-domain public-app evaluation, reliance on XML, and substantial compute requirements.
weaknesses: The main contribution is technically incremental: ADAGRPO combines known ideas such as positive replay, curriculum/filtering of hard instances, and trajectory-length reward shaping on top of GRPO. The paper does not provide a convincing theoretical or empirical argument that these choices are novel beyond this application setting.

The evaluation is not sufficiently trustworthy for the strength of the claims. AndroidWorld has only 116 test tasks and AndroidLab 138 tasks, yet the paper makes broad state-of-the-art claims with limited uncertainty analysis, unclear statistical testing, and only partial averaging over runs.

The AndroidLab training setup is especially concerning: rewards for generated training tasks come from a VLM reward model trained from proprietary-model judgments with only 86% reported accuracy. This makes the RL signal biased and weakens the validity of the reported AndroidLab gains.

The data construction and contamination controls are under-specified. The paper uses human annotations, AndroidControl, generated AndroidLab tasks, and AndroidWorld task variants, but gives only high-level statements about deduplication and non-overlap; this is not enough to rule out leakage or benchmark-specific overfitting.

Baseline comparisons are hard to assess. The paper does not clearly describe whether all baselines were rerun under identical prompts, action spaces, XML inputs, image resolution, temperatures, and evaluation protocols. Comparisons to proprietary and specialized agents therefore may not be apples-to-apples.

The strongest performance appears to depend heavily on supervised fine-tuning and benchmark-specific data, while the RL contribution is smaller and mixed. On AndroidControl, RL actually degrades several metrics, suggesting possible specialization rather than robust general improvement.

Several algorithmic details are unclear or potentially unsound. AdaPR reuses off-policy trajectories inside a GRPO/PPO-style objective without a clear correction or analysis; FCF permanently removes persistently failing tasks, which may bias training away from hard tasks rather than solve them; gamma is reported as 1.0, which seems inconsistent with the claimed mixture of replay and on-policy samples.

There are internal inconsistencies and reproducibility problems. The introduction claims support for over 1,000 environments, while the limitation section says the system stably sustains up to 256 parallel rollouts. The abstract says the framework is open-sourced but leaves the URL blank.

The paper relies on XML accessibility metadata and bounding boxes, which limits generality to real mobile apps where XML is incomplete or unavailable. This weakens the broader claim of general-purpose mobile GUI agents.

Presentation quality is uneven, with formatting errors, missing links, unclear table references, and several imprecise claims. These issues make it harder to verify the method and reproduce the results.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: online reinforcement learning for multi-turn mobile GUI agents, where interactive sampling is expensive and sparse-reward learning is difficult.

The empirical results are strong: MobileRL reports large gains over capable open and proprietary baselines on AndroidWorld and AndroidLab, including 80.2% on AndroidWorld and 53.6% on AndroidLab with a 9B backbone.

The proposed training pipeline is practically compelling. The combination of reasoning-free SFT, reasoning SFT, and online RL is well motivated, and the paper shows stage-wise improvements from each phase.

ADAGRPO is evaluated with useful ablations. AdaPR, SPA, and FCF each appear to contribute, and the additional analyses by task complexity and trajectory length help support the claim that the method improves both success and efficiency.

The paper provides substantial implementation detail in the appendix, including action space, XML preprocessing, hyperparameters, data composition, and limitations. This improves interpretability and partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is moderate rather than deep. Positive replay, curriculum filtering, and length-based reward shaping are sensible adaptations of known ideas to mobile GUI RL, but the paper does not provide much theoretical or conceptual insight beyond this engineering combination.

The AndroidLab training setup raises concerns. Rewards for generated training tasks rely on a VLM reward model trained from proprietary model judgments with only 86% reported accuracy, so some gains may depend on biased or noisy reward supervision rather than verifiable online RL.

The relationship between AndroidWorld-only RL and AndroidLab performance is somewhat confusing. The appendix states that the best MobileRL-9B model is obtained from online RL purely on AndroidWorld, while the main results emphasize AndroidLab gains; clearer separation of transfer, reward-model training, and benchmark-specific training would be important.

Reproducibility remains limited despite many details. The work depends on large human-annotated data, generated AndroidLab training tasks, proprietary VLM judgments, and substantial infrastructure for Android virtual devices; it is unclear whether all needed data, reward models, and code will be released, and the abstract’s open-source link appears blank.

The evaluation is strong but still narrow. AndroidWorld and AndroidLab have small test sets, and the paper does not evaluate out-of-domain public-use apps, which the authors acknowledge. This limits confidence that the method generalizes beyond benchmark-style Android environments and XML-accessible apps.

Baseline comparability is not fully established. Some comparisons appear to use reported results from prior systems with potentially different action spaces, observation formats, prompts, or infrastructure, and more controlled reruns under a unified protocol would strengthen the claims.

The method relies heavily on XML/UI hierarchy and bounding-box action representations. This is practical for current benchmarks but may not transfer to apps with incomplete accessibility metadata or to more vision-only settings.
